newsitem.title: JAPAN: S.Korea urges North to join four-way peace talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea urges North to join four-way peace talks.

text.p: South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha urged hunger-stricken North Korea on Monday to enter proposed four-nation peace talks aimed at a permanent peace on the tension-filled Korean Peninsula.
"It is important to entice North Korea into a forum of dialogue," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official quoted Yoo as telling Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
"The food problem (in North Korea) can be discussed at the four-nation peace talks," Yoo, on a three-day official visit to Japan from Monday, was quoted as saying.
Pyongyang was expected to respond to a proposal for peace talks on Wednesday when a North Korean delegation held another round of preliminary talks with U.S. and South Korean officials in New York.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and his South Korean counterpart Kim Young-sam proposed four-way peace talks one year ago between the two Koreas, the United States and China.

The talks were designed to defuse tensions and eventually bring about a permanent peace on the Korean peninsula, which was divided in the 1950-53 Korean War. The two Koreas remain technically at war since the conflict ended in a truce and not a peace pact.
North Korea has been asking the United States and South Korea for food aid but it was not clear if Pyongyang was trying to make aid a condition for its participation in the four-way peace talks.
South Korea pledged $6 million to the original WFP appeal and the United States $10 million.
Seoul and Washington said they were considering boosting their contribution to the WFP, which is seeking $95.5 million -- up from an initial $41.6 million -- to buy 200,000 tonnes of food.
Japan is holding back. One reason is public anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang.
During Monday's four-hour talks with the Japanese counterpart, South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo said North Korea's economy was worsening.
"The North Korean economy continues to get worse," Yoo was quoted as saying.

Noting reports that a total of 122 North Korean army officers were promoted, Yoo said the communist state's de facto leader Kim Jong-il was "attaching importance to the military". He did not elaborate.

Kim Jong-il, supreme commander of the country's 1.1-million-strong military, has yet to be formally confirmed in two key posts held by his late father -- general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
North Korea watchers believe Kim Jong-il is likely to formally assume the posts this year after the third anniversary of his father's death in July.
